ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣлъка (bělŭka, “squirrel”), diminutive of бѣла (běla, “squirrel”) (see -ка (-ka)), from бѣла вѣверица (běla věverica, “white squirrel”), from Proto-Slavic *bělъka. See бе́лый (bélyj, “white”), ве́верица (véverica, “squirrel; ermine, stoat”).

From бро́сить (brósitʹ, “to throw”) + -кий (-kij). Compary typologically Czech nápadný; Bulgarian биещ на очи (biešt na oči), броса́ться в глаза́ (brosátʹsja v glazá). Also compare неотрази́мый (neotrazímyj), Polish rażący; захва́тывающий (zaxvátyvajuščij), English catchy.

ety.text: Modification of older керза (kerza), borrowed from English kersey (“type of rough woolen cloth”). Popularly etymologized as an abbreviation of ки́ровский заво́д (kírovskij zavód, “Kirov factory”), where it supposedly was first made.

ety.text: Borrowed from English condom. The pronunciation as кондо́м instead of ко́ндом could be an influence by German Kondom. Became more common after 1990 through coverage of the HIV/AIDS pandemic, though attested from at least 1886 in medical literature; it became popularly mispronounced as гондо́н (gondón), now vulgar.

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙋтъка (utŭka), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtъka, diminutive of *ǫty. By surface analysis, уть (utʹ) + -ка (-ka). Cognate to Lithuanian antis, Germanic ant, and, Latin anas.
Probably of expressive origin, also reminiscent of words like *koxati (“to love”).
